The core insight the exam rewards: evals are code. They live in the repo, run in CI, block bad merges, and get the same review rigor as application code. A team that "evals manually sometimes" has no evals.

How to read this diagram
  1. Prompt change (left): any change enters here: a prompt edit, a model version bump, a chunking change, new tools. All changes are suspects until proven innocent.
  2. Eval run: the system executes the full golden dataset against the changed system, in a sandbox with production-like data.
  3. Golden data (cylinder): This is the versioned dataset of inputs. It has known-good answers. This is the ground truth. The system measures everything against it.
  4. LLM judge (gavel): a model scores each output against a rubric. Fast and scalable, but itself a model with biases, so it needs calibration.
  5. Gate: The system compares scores to thresholds. It also compares scores to the previous run. A pass deploys. A fail loops back to the engineer. It shows a diff of what regressed.
  6. Production watch (below): The system samples live traffic. It scores the traffic continuously. Drift here creates new golden cases. So the dataset grows with reality.

Golden datasets

What they are: The system curates these sets of inputs. They have known-good outputs. The system stores them in version control with the code. How to build one:

How to read this diagram
  1. Each pair has a query. It has the known-good answer. It has the context. The system judged it against the context.
  2. The system freezes and versions the set. It has the same pairs. It has the same answers. This is true for every run.
  3. 50 to 200 pairs cover a domain. Fewer is a spot check, not an eval.
  4. New failures become new pairs: the set grows where the system bleeds.

What breaks if a part fails: If the model under test writes the golden answers, the evaluation grades its own homework.

  • Start from production: sample real user inputs, anonymize them, and have domain experts write or approve the reference answers. Real inputs beat imagined ones; your users' weird phrasings are the test that matters.
  • Cover the shape of the problem: every document type, every tool, every language you support. Include the hard cases on purpose: ambiguous questions, multi-hop questions, and questions with no good answer (the system must refuse cleanly).
  • Size honestly: 200 to 500 cases is the working range for most systems. Fewer than 100 and noise dominates: a 3-point swing might be two lucky cases. Thousands are better but cost real expert time; grow the set from production failures instead of guessing.
  • Version everything: the dataset, the rubric, and the judge prompt are all versioned. When scores move, you must be able to answer "did the system change or did the test change".

LLM-as-judge

What it is: Use a language model to score outputs. This is for cases where exact-match checking does not work. Many good ways exist to write a correct answer. Here is how it works under the hood: The judge receives the input. The judge receives the system's output. The judge receives the reference answer.

The judge also receives a rubric. The rubric has concrete criteria. An example is "2 points: cites the correct document section". Another example is "1 point: answer is correct but uncited". Another example is "0 points: contradicts the reference". It returns scores.

It also returns a short justification.

How to read this diagram
  1. VIBES: "this looks good." Unrepeatable, unarguable, untestable.
  2. RUBRIC: named criteria, each scored 1 to 5, with what each score means written down.
  3. The judge reads the rubric, not your hopes. Calibrate it against human scores first.
  4. A rubric turns "the model got worse" into "faithfulness fell from 4.2 to 3.1 on claims without sources."

What breaks if a part fails: If the judge has no rubric, its scores drift with its mood and the trend line is noise.

Decisions that matter:

  • Rubric over vibes: "rate this answer 1 to 5" produces noise. A rubric with named criteria and point values produces repeatable scores. Write the rubric before you need it, and review it like code.
  • Calibrate against humans: have humans score 100 outputs, have the judge score the same 100, and measure agreement. If the judge agrees with humans less than ~85 percent of the time, fix the rubric or the judge before trusting the pipeline. Re-calibrate whenever the judge model changes.
  • Know the biases: judges favor longer answers, answers that sound confident, and answers in the style of their own model family. Counter with rubrics that penalize verbosity and with spot-check audits.
  • Judge tier: a strong model judges more accurately but costs more per eval run. Many teams judge with a mid-tier model and reserve human review for disagreements and for the highest-stakes cases. See Design 8 for the pricing logic.

CI gates

What they are: The system automates these checks. They run on every pull request. They block merging when quality regresses. The gate rules, concrete:

How to read this diagram
  1. Faithfulness gate: every claim needs a retrieved source. Fails on hallucinated citations.
  2. Regression gate: golden-set pass rate must not fall below the frozen baseline.
  3. Latency gate: p95 stays under the SLA.
  4. Cost gate: per-query cost stays inside the budget.

What breaks if a part fails: If the gates run after the merge, they are a newsletter, not a gate.

  • Accuracy floor: overall score must stay above the committed threshold (for example, 90 percent faithfulness on the RAG golden set).
  • No per-segment regression: No document type may drop more than 2 percentage points. No tool may drop more than 2 percentage points. No query category may drop more than 2 percentage points. This is true from the previous run. This is true even if the overall score holds. This is the contract-review lesson from the blueprint.
    An overall 96 percent score hid a failing segment.
  • Latency ceiling: p95 end-to-end latency on the eval set must stay under the SLA (for example, 8 seconds). A prompt that is 2 points more accurate but 3x slower fails the gate.
  • Cost ceiling: mean tokens per task must stay within budget. A "better" prompt that doubles token usage is a cost regression.
  • Safety checks: a dedicated slice of adversarial cases (prompt injection attempts, disallowed content requests) must pass at 100 percent. Safety is not averaged; it is binary.

How it runs in practice: the PR pipeline spins up the changed system. It runs the golden set (parallelized, typically minutes). It posts a score diff as a PR comment ("faithfulness 91.2 percent, up 0.8; p95 latency 6.1 s, up 0.4 s; ticket-tools segment down 2.3 points, FAILING"). It blocks merge on any red rule. The engineer sees exactly what regressed and where.

Monitoring and alerting in production

Evals in CI test the system you built. Monitoring tests the system your users meet. The two differ because production brings inputs you never imagined.

How to read this diagram
  1. The system samples judge scores in production. This includes faithfulness. This includes relevance. This includes tone.
  2. Trend the scores, not the level. A slow drift is the killer.
  3. Alert on the slope: three bad days in a row pages someone.
  4. Every alert links to the trace: the exact inputs that produced the bad answer.

What breaks if a part fails: If monitoring watches uptime only, quality can decay for months while every dashboard stays green.

  • Sample live traffic: score a random 5 percent of production interactions with the judge pipeline nightly. Track the trend, not just the level: a slow 1-point-per-week decay is data drift, and it is invisible without the trend line.
  • Log everything structured: every request logs the prompt version, model version, tools called, tokens used, latency per stage, and the final output. When something breaks at 3 AM, this log is the difference between diagnosis and guessing.
  • Alert on: Alert on judge-score drops beyond a threshold. Alert on spikes in refusal rate. The system suddenly cannot answer. Alert on spikes in tool error rate. Alert on latency p95 breaching SLA. Alert on cost per task jumping.
    This is a prompt change that doubled output tokens.
  • Close the loop: every production failure that the golden set missed becomes a new golden case. The dataset is a living record of every mistake the system has made, which is why it keeps working.

Worked example: what the pipeline costs

Illustrative: 300 golden cases, each a RAG query costing ~$0.014 (from Design 1), judged by a mid-tier model at ~$0.01 per judgment. One full eval run: 300 x $0.024 = $7.20. Ten PRs a day each running evals: $72 per day, about $2,160 per month. Nightly production sampling of 5 percent of 10,000 daily requests (500 judged): 500 x $0.01 = $5 per day. Total eval spend under $2,500 per month to guard a system that costs $5,000+ per month to run and whose failures cost customers. The exam's framing: evals are not overhead, they are the cheapest insurance in the architecture.

How they will ask this

Exam angle

The blueprint's D4 is the exam's third-largest domain. It defines evaluation metrics. It designs datasets with mixed methodologies. It runs A/B tests. It diagnoses issues. It monitors with logging.

Expect the contract-review shape directly. An aggregate metric looks fine. One segment fails. The credited move is per-segment measurement. Fix the weak segment before go-live.

Expect judge design. The wrong answers are "have the LLM rate outputs 1 to 5". This has no rubric. Another wrong answer is "trust the judge completely". This has no calibration. The credited answer pairs a rubric with human-agreement calibration.

Expect CI gating. This is a scenario where a prompt change ships without evaluations. Quality drops. The fix is the gate with accuracy rules. It also has per-segment rules. It also has latency rules.

It also has cost rules. It also has safety rules.

A question mentions diagnosing hallucinations. A question mentions diagnosing prompt failures. First, use the structured logs. The prompt version tells you about the failure. The retrieved chunks tell you about the failure. The tool traces tell you whether the failure is retrieval, reasoning, or data.

The trap to retire: "An uncalibrated LLM judge is not an evaluation. It is an opinion with a score attached." The exam will offer "add an LLM judge" as a complete answer. This is for an evaluation-design question. The credited answer always includes the rubric. It always includes the human-agreement calibration. Without them, the scores are not trustworthy.

Next: Design 8. The master framework that ties every design's trade-offs together: cost, latency, quality.

Design 8 Cost / Latency / Quality: The Master Framework

Why this comes next. Designs 1 through 7 each made local trade-offs: this retrieval strategy, that failover door, this cache policy. Design 8 answers the meta-question: one framework for the cost, latency, and quality trilemma, applied back across all seven designs.

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version.

Every design in this guide is a point on one triangle. This chapter gives you the framework, the numbers, and the decision rules, then applies them back across all seven designs.

                          QUALITY
                          (Opus)
                         /        \
                        /  Sonnet  \
                       /  (center)  \
                      /______________\
                 COST                LATENCY
                (Haiku)              (Haiku)
  rule: read the binding constraint --> pick the CHEAPEST tier that satisfies it
  cheat: tier the workload (cheap bulk, strong hard slice) + cache + batch

The master framework

As you learned in D1, every design is a trade-off. The triangle makes the trade-off visible: push one corner and the other two move.

How to read this diagram
  1. Each corner is a pressure: quality up, cost and latency down.
  2. Your design is a point inside. A cheaper model moves you toward the cost corner.
  3. Push one corner and the other two push back. Name the binding constraint first.

What breaks if a part fails: if you optimize without naming the binding constraint, you will trade away the thing the business actually needed.

What the trilemma is: cost, latency, and quality pull in three directions. You can optimize any two comfortably; the third pays. A cheap, fast system will not be the smartest. The smartest, cheapest system will not be fast. The framework turns this from a slogan into a decision procedure.

How to read this diagram
  1. Simple, high-volume tasks: the smallest tier that clears the quality bar.
  2. Standard tasks: the middle tier. Hard reasoning: the top tier.
  3. Task difficulty climbs the ladder. Prestige does not climb the ladder.
  4. Route each query to the cheapest tier that passes: that is the whole cost strategy.

What breaks if a part fails: If every query climbs to the top tier, you pay flagship prices for commodity answers.

How to read this diagram
  1. The three corners: COST (bottom left), LATENCY (bottom right), QUALITY (top). Moving toward a corner means prioritizing that dimension.
  2. Haiku (bottom edge): the small, fast, cheap tier. Near both the cost and latency corners, far from quality. Right for high-volume, narrow tasks.
  3. Sonnet (center): the balanced tier. The default for agents, RAG generation, and judges. Good at everything, best at nothing.
  4. Opus (top corner): the flagship tier. Maximum reasoning quality, highest cost, slowest. Right when a mistake costs more than the tokens.
  5. The caption, "pick two": the honest summary. If a scenario demands all three, the answer is architecture (caching, routing, tiering), not a single model choice.

The decision procedure:

  1. Read the constraints first. The scenario states the constraints. An accuracy SLA is a constraint. A latency budget is a constraint. A cost ceiling is a constraint. A compliance rule is a constraint.
    Rank the constraints.
    Find the binding constraint. Find the nice-to-have constraints.
  2. Translate constraints to the triangle. "p95 under 2 seconds" pins you near the latency corner. "95 percent accuracy on contracts" pins you near quality. "$0.01 per request ceiling" pins you near cost.
  3. Pick the cheapest point that satisfies the binding constraint. Never buy more quality than the SLA needs; never buy more speed than the budget needs. Over-engineering is a wrong answer on this exam.
  4. Use architecture to cheat the triangle. Caching moves you toward cheap without losing quality. Routing (small model first, escalate hard cases) moves you toward cheap without losing quality on average. Async batch moves you toward cheap when latency does not matter.

Model tier pricing (illustrative)

Table 8.1: Verified September 2026 against Anthropic's pricing docs (Haiku 4.5 $1/$5, Sonnet 5 $2/$10, Opus 5.5 $4/$20, Fable 5.1 $10/$50 per million tokens). Ratios to teach: output costs ~5x input; each tier costs roughly 2x the one below. The exam tests trade-off logic, not memorized numbers.

Tier Input (illustrative $/MTok) Output (illustrative $/MTok) Relative speed Reach for it when
Haiku class (small) ~$1 ~$5 Fastest Classification, extraction, simple Q/A, high-volume filtering, subagent workers
Sonnet class (mid) ~$2 ~$10 Medium Agents, RAG generation, judges, general production default
Opus class (flagship) ~$4 ~$20 Slowest Hard reasoning, legal/financial accuracy SLAs, the 5 percent of cases that decide outcomes

Three pricing levers beyond tier choice:

  • Prompt caching (Design 5): 90 percent off repeated input prefixes. The single biggest lever for agentic and RAG workloads with stable prompts.
  • Batch API: roughly 50 percent off for async workloads with no latency requirement (results in hours, not seconds). Overnight eval runs, bulk classification, and backfills belong here.
  • Output discipline: Output tokens cost ~5x input tokens. "Answer in one sentence" cuts the most expensive tokens first. So does structured JSON instead of prose. So does refusing to generate when the answer is "not found."

Token budgets and p95 latency targets

Translate money and time into per-request budgets before you design. Worked from the designs above:

Workload Token budget / request p95 latency target How it is met
Support chat (RAG) ~3,000 in / 300 out 8 s Mid-tier model, rerank top-5 only, cached system prompt
Helpdesk agent turn ~4,000 in / 400 out per turn, max 10 turns 10 s per turn (approval wait excluded) Mid-tier model, 6 focused tools (cached definitions), tool timeouts
Extraction subagent ~3,000 in / 300 out 120 s (background) Small-tier model, parallel fan-out
Brief writer + critic ~20,000 in / 4,000 out 10 min (background) Mid-tier for draft, mid-tier judge, one revise loop max
Eval judge per case ~2,000 in / 200 out Batch (Batch API, 50% off) Mid-tier judge, overnight runs
Contract review (95% SLA) As needed Minutes (async) Flagship tier: the SLA prices the tier, not the other way around

Reading the table: Latency targets come from the user experience. Chat must feel instant. Background jobs must finish before the meeting. Token budgets come from the cost ceiling. Divide the cost ceiling by volume.

budget_per_request = daily_cost_ceiling / requests_per_day

Where: daily_cost_ceiling = $500; requests_per_day = 50,000.

A scenario gives you "50,000 requests per day". It also gives you "$500 per day". Your per-request budget is $0.01. That number alone rules out uniform flagship usage. This is true before you read another word.

Applied across the designs

  • Design 1 (RAG): mid-tier for generation, hosted reranker for precision, caching on the stable prompt. The rerank spend ($0.002/query) is the cheapest quality on the menu. Quality binding: faithfulness above 90 percent. Cost guard: top-5 not top-10 chunks.
  • Design 2 (agent): mid-tier for the loop, small-tier for sub-classification steps (intent routing). Capability-bloat control doubles as cost control: fewer tool definitions, fewer input tokens, every turn. Latency binding: 10 s per turn via tool timeouts.
  • Design 3 (multi-agent): small-tier for 50 extraction workers, flagship-tier for orchestration, writing, and the final critic pass on high-stakes briefs. This tiering is what makes 50 parallel agents cost about $0.40 instead of about $0.90 on flagship.
  • Design 4 (MCP): cost lives in the host's prompt (tool schemas cached) and in audit log storage. The security boundary is non-negotiable regardless of tier: never trade the OAuth and least-privilege controls for cost.
  • Design 5 (caching): the triangle cheat code. Moves any design toward the cost corner without moving away from quality, provided reuse beats the TTL. Always price the break-even before enabling.
  • Design 6 (failover): the standby providers cost little until used, but the failover minute costs full input price while caches rewarm. Budget the rewarm, pin versions, and never let a cost-saving failover cross a residency boundary.
  • Design 7 (evaluations): Use a batch API for nightly evaluations. This is 50 percent off. There is no latency need. Use mid-tier judges. Use human review only for disagreements. Evaluation spend stays under approximately 5 percent of serving spend.
    Above that, you over-test.

The one-paragraph trilemma summary

Find the binding constraint. Buy the cheapest tier that satisfies it. Tier the workload. Cheap models do the bulk. Strong models do the hard slice. Cache every stable prefix.

Batch everything without a latency requirement. Measure per segment. Gate every change. Never let a cost optimization cross a safety line. Never let a cost optimization cross a residency line. Never let a cost optimization cross an accuracy-SLA line.

That paragraph answers a third of this exam.

How to read this diagram
  1. The bulk tier (left): cheap small models do the high-volume work: extraction, filtering, classification.
  2. The hard slice (right): the strong model handles only the cases that need real reasoning: orchestration, the final critic pass.
  3. The worked numbers: 50 parallel extraction agents cost about $0.40 tiered on the small tier instead of flagship prices on all of them. Routing by difficulty is the cheapest architecture move in the guide.

What breaks if a part fails: If the hard slice goes to the cheap tier, you will pay back the savings. You will pay back the savings as quality failures.

How they will ask this

How to read this diagram
  1. Each row pairs a design with its question shape: RAG asks chunking versus data shape; caching asks the break-even judgment.
  2. Learn the SHAPE, not just the facts. The scenario changes; the angle repeats.
  3. Constraint-first reading works on every row: find the rule in the scenario, then pick the control.

What breaks if a part fails: if you memorize facts without the angles, a reworded scenario will look like a brand-new topic.

Exam angle

The blueprint's D1 objective is to align solutions to business value pillars: efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, and performance SLAs. D4 covers token usage, latency, and cost-performance trade-offs. Expect the classic scenario: 10,000 daily requests, a $0.02 per-request ceiling, and a 95 percent accuracy SLA. The distractors are: flagship everywhere (blows the cost), small model everywhere (blows the SLA), or caching a unique-per-request prompt (no reuse).

The credited answer tiers the workload. A small model filters and routes. A mid-tier model handles the standard cases with caching. A flagship model takes only the escalated hard cases. Per-segment evaluations prove the SLA holds. Two answers both satisfy the constraint.

Pick the cheaper one. An answer satisfies cost but breaks the SLA. It is wrong no matter how cheap. Constraint first, price second, always.

The trap to retire: "'Use the best model everywhere' fails two ways. It blows the cost ceiling. It blows the latency budget. Flagship models are slower." The exam's credited answers almost always tier the workload. Cheap models are for the bulk. Strong models are for the hard slice.

Uniform tiering is the expensive distractor.
